quote: A single fleeting image can be enough to prime associated words for recognition. Don’t think it takes anything more to set confirmation bias in motion.
content: "One quick flash, and the bottom line is already decided" overreaches, and the behavioural-priming collapse is real. But the essay's chain from recognition to judgment does not run through elderly walking or money primes, none of which it cites. It runs through its own cited experiment: the anchor question primed anchor-consistent knowledge, measured by lexical decision, and that knowledge moved the estimate (Mussweiler & Strack). The lexical-decision measure there is the mechanism of a judgment effect, anchoring, which Many Labs replicated in every sample (Klein et al. 2014). Recognition priming bears on judgment through selective accessibility, which is robust. The claim Fable attacks belongs to a literature the essay did not use.

quote: But someone must be, because these signs have been shown to work, which is why stores keep putting them up.
content: This is conceded. A Wansink citation cannot carry "have been shown," and the line needs another source or a softer verb. The store-sign point can stand as a hypothesis. Stores do test their promotions, so "which is why stores keep putting them up" is weak evidence, stronger than a lottery buyer's willingness to pay, since a retailer who tests is measuring the effect and the buyer is not. It is still not a demonstration, and the essay should not have called it one. Fable's criticism here holds as stated.

quote: confirmation bias is built directly into our hardware, associational networks priming compatible thoughts and memories
content: The essay's own cited experiment settles this. After the 5 °C anchor, subjects were faster on "cold" and "snow," and after the 20 °C anchor faster on "hot" and "sun." The activation was not symmetric across antonyms. It was selective for whatever was consistent with the hypothesis being tested, which is why the model is named selective accessibility. Semantic networks may be symmetric at rest. A hypothesis under consideration directs retrieval toward instances that fit it, and that is the positive-test strategy found in hypothesis testing generally (Snyder & Swann 1978). Nickerson's review lists exactly this selective retrieval of confirming instances among the forms of confirmation bias. The property Fable says is missing is in the essay's citation.
